quote: Nobody really says goodbye.
why: reports an absent reaction as proof the leaving is ordinary instead of showing the scene's actual texture
suggestion: Cut it and open on the concrete detail: "The loop out front is full of cars with their trunks standing open."

quote: Nobody says anything to her the whole time.
why: uses an absent group reaction as evidence the isolation is normal, the exact banned normalizing device
suggestion: Cut the line and let the silence live in her sitting with her hands in her lap for the rest of the period.

quote: “I don’t know”
why: the same line is repeated verbatim by the same speaker immediately after, adding no new information
suggestion: Let the first "I don't know" stand alone, or replace the second with a different, broken fragment: "I don't—"

quote: It's out of her before she has hold of any of it.
why: explains that the line was involuntary right after the dialogue already showed her blurting it out unbidden
suggestion: Cut the sentence and let "It's kind of like mailing something to a stranger" stand on its own.

quote: He isn't being mean about it. He's saying what he can see.
why: restates the non-meanness the tag "interested" and the inherited simile already conveyed
suggestion: Cut both sentences; the delivery and the shoe-untied comparison already carry it.

quote: there are more adults in it than Chloe has seen in one place all month, and somebody's little brother is screaming about a shoe
why: two "and"s chain three unrelated observations at equal weight instead of ranking them
suggestion: The loop out front is full of cars with their trunks standing open, more adults in it than Chloe has seen in one place all month, somebody's little brother screaming about a shoe.

quote: Chloe comes in and stands at the end of the counter and waits until there's a gap in it
why: three actions are chained by two "and"s with no hierarchy between them
suggestion: as Chloe comes in and stands at the end of the counter, waiting until there's a gap in it

quote: She goes and gets the phone book out from under the microwave and puts it on the counter.
why: three verbs (goes, gets, puts) sit side by side with equal grammatical weight
suggestion: She gets the phone book from under the microwave and puts it on the counter.

quote: sits down on the end of her bed and thinks and tries to remember
why: three verbs chained by "and" flatten a build toward the rendered memory that follows
suggestion: She goes upstairs and sits on the end of her bed, trying to remember.

quote: then Chloe's name, then says yes, that's the one, then listens for a long stretch
why: three "then"s chain a phone call's beats at equal weight, the exact construction the rule names
suggestion: gives their name, then Chloe's, confirms yes, that's the one, and settles into a long stretch of listening

quote: finish first and sit still and not say anything to anybody at her table
why: two "and"s chain three behaviors at equal weight instead of showing the routine has a hierarchy
suggestion: finish first, sit still, and say nothing to anybody at her table

quote: reads the top of the page, and then reads the top of the page again, and puts it down on the floor
why: the repeated reading and the giving-up are chained as equal, same-weight items
suggestion: reads the top of the page, reads it again, then gives up and puts it down on the floor

quote: and puts the phone down and stands with her hand still on it
why: two "and"s chain three actions with no clause depending on another
suggestion: puts the phone down and stands there, her hand still on it

quote: and crouches all the way down beside the desk, in front of everybody, and puts a hand flat on Chloe's back and leaves it there
why: three "and"s chain four actions of very different weight (crouching in front of the class vs. leaving a hand in place) as if equal
suggestion: crouches all the way down beside the desk, in front of everybody, and puts a hand flat on Chloe's back, leaving it there

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
quote: so when is the part where you're done thinking about it.
why: this line sits inside a run of six dialogue turns (lines 169-179) with no physical beat anywhere between them
suggestion: Drop in one anchor, e.g. "Chloe stands in the doorway in her pajamas," partway through the run.

quote: Bryce says it interested
why: the adjective "interested" is used as an adverb after "says it," the exact banned construction
suggestion: Bryce says it, leaning in a little, like he's actually curious.

quote: her eyes start to get wet
why: a generic physiological cliche for imminent crying that could belong to any anxious child in any scene
suggestion: her chin tucks down and she scrubs the back of her wrist across one eye

quote: she looks about to start to cry
why: another generic, unspecific description of imminent crying with no detail rooted in this character or moment
suggestion: her mouth goes tight at the corners, the way it does right before

quote: she knows exactly what he sounds like when he laughs
why: routes the memory through the filter verb "knows" instead of rendering the sound directly
suggestion: and she can still hear it, two short barks and then his hand over his mouth

quote: She can hear herself still going
why: filters her own continuing speech through the perception verb "hear" instead of just letting the words keep coming
suggestion: She keeps going anyway.

quote: she knows what it actually means
why: routes the realization through the filter verb "knows" instead of rendering what the realization actually is
suggestion: By the end of the month, "we're thinking about it" means nothing is coming.

quote: Then she sees Chloe in the doorway with the glass.
why: routes the moment through the filter verb "sees" instead of rendering Chloe's presence directly
suggestion: Then Chloe is in the doorway with the glass.

quote: doing something with the mail
why: "something" stands in for a concrete action the narrator could simply name
suggestion: doing something with the mail

quote: there is nothing left in the sheet to be inside
why: near-verbatim match to the rule's own banned example ("nothing left in the worksheet to find out"), a vague abstraction standing in for the actual feeling
suggestion: she has checked every answer twice and the page has nothing left to give her

quote: She thinks about how she was doing fractions at the camp
why: states that she thought about the camp instead of rendering the thought's own rhythm or interruption
suggestion: Fractions at camp—staying up, the number finally sitting still on the page—and now this.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a moment
why: a vague universal duration marker from the same crutch family ("for a second"/"for a while") the rule names, used regardless of what's actually being timed
suggestion: Chloe's mouth opens, then stays open a beat too long.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything

why: one of two more "for a second" instances in this chapter beyond the ones already flagged, the exact phrase the rule bans as a universal duration marker

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: these things take a while

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second before she answers
why: the exact banned universal duration marker "for a second"

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything

why: the exact banned universal duration marker "for a second," used as filler rather than a real beat
suggestion: The librarian looks at her over the top of the card. "That's a real month, that is,"

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: it takes her a second
why: the same vague "a second" duration filler recurring a third time in this chapter

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the part where you're done thinking about it
why: "the part where" is named directly in the rule as a placeholder for behavior that should be shown instead of labeled
suggestion: so when are you done

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while.
why: the exact banned universal duration marker "for a while"
suggestion: She listens without saying anything, the pen tapping twice against the envelope.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: would really like to talk to them
why: "really" softens a claim with no honest uncertainty behind it, pure filler intensifier
suggestion: that Chloe would like to talk to them

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: just her two books
why: "just" softens a fact the narrator states with total certainty (exactly two books), padding rather than hedging
suggestion: Chloe comes out with her two books she hadn't finished.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: to just renew them
why: "just" pads a plainly stated request the narrator is certain about
suggestion: asks her mom to renew them please

quote: it was hard
why: "it was" plus a bare adjective tells the reader fractions were difficult instead of dramatizing the difficulty
suggestion: because fractions had taken her four tries the first time

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
quote: being extremely polite in the voice that means she has already been given the answer and is going to hear it one more time
why: a long, multi-step social inference about bureaucratic tone held in one breath is beyond what an eight-year-old's perception would track, and the sentence structure itself doesn't shorten for her
suggestion: Her mom's voice goes careful, the way it does when she already knows what's coming.

quote: "We're all getting in, I promise"
why: the line closes with no terminal punctuation before the closing quotation mark
suggestion: "We're all getting in, I promise."

quote: "Oh," Her mom puts the envelope down.
why: stray capitalization after the comma; the sentence should continue lowercase or the comma should be a period
suggestion: "Oh," her mom puts the envelope down.

quote: Chloe looks confused for a moment, "I don't know his number."
why: a comma splices a bare narrative fragment directly to a self-contained, terminally-punctuated line of dialogue, the exact construction the rulebook names as a fail
suggestion: Chloe looks confused for a moment. "I don't know his number."

quote: She opens it while looking at Chloe, "What's his last name sweetie?"
why: comma splices a narrative clause directly to a self-contained line of dialogue instead of using a period or a proper tag
suggestion: She opens it while looking at Chloe. "What's his last name, sweetie?"

quote: She comes back down, “I don’t know?”
why: comma splices a bare narrative fragment to a self-contained, terminally-punctuated line of dialogue
suggestion: She comes back down. "I don't know?"

quote: "Ruth, the one you said built a better bridge?," her mom asks.
why: a stray comma follows the question mark before the attribution tag, which needs neither
suggestion: "Ruth, the one you said built a better bridge?" her mom asks.

quote: either", her eyes start to get wet.
why: the comma sits outside the closing quotation mark, inconsistent with the convention used correctly elsewhere in this chapter (e.g. line 47)
suggestion: "I don't know Kavi's either," her eyes start to get wet.

quote: school”, and then she closes the phone book
why: the comma sits outside the closing curly quotation mark, inconsistent with the style guide's own passing example of this exact construction
suggestion: “It’s OK, we can just ask the school,” and then she closes the phone book

quote: "Right, no, I understand that," She listens again.
why: stray capitalization on "She" after the comma; the continuation should be lowercase
suggestion: "Right, no, I understand that," she listens again.

quote: Thank you very much.", and hangs up.
why: a period inside the closing quotation mark is immediately followed by a comma outside it, a stacked, non-standard punctuation error
suggestion: "Thank you very much." And she hangs up.

quote: for a second,"That's a real month
why: a missing space between the comma and the opening quotation mark interrupts the line
suggestion: for a second, "That's a real month

quote: “I don’t know”, she tries to stop
why: the comma sits outside the closing curly quotation mark, inconsistent with correct usage elsewhere in the chapter
suggestion: “I don’t know,” she tries to stop, but she can’t.

quote: Then she sees Chloe in the doorway with the glass.
why: this moment is her mom's perception of Chloe, not something Chloe herself can see or hear, breaking the close-third POV on Chloe
suggestion: Her mom's hand comes off the phone, and her eyes find Chloe in the doorway with the glass.

quote: has hold of any of it
why: "it" (her own half-formed thought) is handed the physical verb "hold," reifying an abstraction as an object that can be grasped
suggestion: before she can stop herself

quote: fifth grade is a rumor
why: a newly invented, writerly metaphor appearing in narration rather than in a character's mouth
suggestion: because nobody in the room has ever seen fifth grade

quote: for the first time
why: "for the first time" is a narrator superlative, explicitly listed as fine in dialogue but banned in narration
suggestion: She asks on a Sunday, in the car, coming back from her grandmother's.

quote: He is seven and a half
why: opens a run of five consecutive sentences all beginning "He...", well past the three-beat anaphora limit the rule bans
suggestion: He is seven and a half, sleeps with the window open, has a sister or maybe a cousin who plays soccer, and can swim two lengths without stopping.

quote: because it was hard
why: explains something the preceding clause ("had to stay up late to figure it out") already made obvious
suggestion: and how she had to stay up late to figure it out

quote: She asks in the car on the way to school and again on the way home.
why: "asks" is used as the frame verb five times in two sentences (asking, asks, asks, asks again, ask), the repeated-frame-verb construction the rule bans
suggestion: She asks at breakfast, in the car both ways, over her mom's shoulder on the phone, and again from the stairs after bedtime.

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
quote: the room takes nineteen minutes
why: a hyper-precise duration deployed on a mundane classroom wait with no characterizing purpose, the narration defaulting to the tic rather than using it as a signal
suggestion: and waits for the room to catch up around her
